#10663. Brain-inspired chip runs near absolute zero and could transform quantum computing

Researchers at the University of Hong Kong (HKU) have unveiled a significant advance in cryogenic electronics that could help overcome key challenges in quantum computing and support future deep space missions. The team, from HKU's Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering and the Centre for Advanced Semiconductors and Integrated Circuits (CASIC), developed a programmable neuromorphic hardware platform capable of operating at temperatures near absolute zero.

The research was led by Professor Yuhao Zhang and PhD student Xin Yang. Their work introduces a new method for generating and controlling negative differential resistance (NDR) in industry standard Silicon Carbide (SiC) MOSFETs. Using this approach, the researchers demonstrated for the first time that a single transistor can reproduce the energy efficient "spiking" activity of biological neurons at temperatures as low as 10mK.

Brain-Inspired Hardware for Quantum Computing

Quantum computers depend on sophisticated control electronics to manage qubits, which are highly sensitive and must be kept at millikelvin temperatures. Existing silicon based control systems consume considerable power and produce unwanted heat, making it necessary to position them away from the qubits themselves. That distance creates extensive wiring requirements that can hinder performance and make large scale quantum computers more difficult to build.

"Our work introduces a hardware platform that can be integrated alongside quantum processors," said Professor Zhang. "By using the unique carrier dynamics in silicon carbide, we can create circuits that are thousands of times more energy-efficient than conventional electronics, significantly reducing the thermal load on cryogenic systems."

Silicon Carbide Reveals Unique Cryogenic Behavior

The team found that SiC MOSFETs display a strong "S-shape" NDR effect when cooled below 2K. This behavior is driven by electron-donor impact ionization (EDII). Unlike other technologies that depend on heat generated within a device, the newly observed mechanism arises directly from the material's atomic properties. As a result, it remains highly stable and can be reproduced consistently across different manufacturing batches.

"This is a robust and scalable approach," said Mr. Yang. "Because SiC is already used globally in electric vehicles and power grids, we can leverage existing industrial foundries to manufacture these cryogenic chips on 300-mm wafers."

From Artificial Neurons to Deep Space Missions

The study also demonstrated that these artificial neurons can be linked together, or "cascaded," into larger networks. This capability could enable advanced local data processing at cryogenic temperatures and improve important quantum computing functions such as quantum error correction and real time quantum control.

The potential applications extend well beyond quantum computing. Because the circuits are designed to operate reliably in extremely cold environments, they could also be valuable for deep space exploration. Future systems may be able to function in the harsh conditions found on the Moon's surface or in the distant regions of our solar system.

The findings were published in Nature Communications in a paper titled "Cryogenic neuromorphic circuits using gate-controlled negative differential resistance in silicon carbide."

Pokemon TCG collectors are raising concerns after an AliExpress listing appeared to offer custom PSA-style labels for almost any card, complete with front and back designs, barcodes, QR codes and a holographic patch.

The AliExpress listing was shown in a video shared by collectibles commentator Max Long. It appeared to be priced at $4.05, with more than 5,000 sales displayed on the page. The product is advertised as a customizable label rather than a PSA-graded collectible, but collectors fear the designs could be placed on raw cards and resold as genuine slabs.

You can go on AliExpress and make your own PSA labels? 😬 pic.twitter.com/9rkmSDEv8d

The concern grew after Japanese Pokemon card collector Pokemonlana posted screenshots of the same style of label using two different PSA certification numbers.

One was printed on a Dark Persian front label, while the reverse used a separate number. The collector questioned how buyers could distinguish the copies from real PSA labels and pointed out that buyers had left positive reviews on the listing.

ちょっと待ってよwPSAのラベルコピー品売ってるのかよwwwクオリティ高くて本物と見分けるのどうしたらいいの？もう怖くて買えないw購入した方のコメントも満足度高めで草wwww pic.twitter.com/JoVOMxzAFQ

Roman Pioneer, founder of the authentication database CheckCOA, examined the listing and similar products after the posts began circulating. His investigation found AliExpress stores offering custom front and back labels alongside unsealed card cases.

One store, called BEST REPLICA LABELS YOU’LL FIND, advertised a “DIY custom rating card label” and had reportedly sold 170 units with a 4.7-star rating.

Buyer photos showed labels using PSA certification numbers tied to a Paldean Fates Mew ex and a Rocket Dark Gyarados. Both numbers corresponded to real PSA records, meaning a buyer who only checks the certification number could see a genuine card description and grade.

A second store, High Quality Cards Store, advertised custom labels made from details supplied by the buyer. Its product video showed a copied PSA label being tilted under a light so the silver patch reflected in a similar way to the security feature on a genuine label.

PSA confirms FBI investigating $1 million Pokemon & trading card heist as full stolen list revealed

One label used a deactivated PSA number, while another used an active certification number for a GEM MT 10 One Piece Zoro card.

PSA itself warns that checking a certification number does not eliminate the risk of buying a counterfeit collectible. The company says counterfeiters can copy real numbers from public records and encourages buyers to compare cards with PSA’s own images, inspect the case for signs of tampering and purchase from trusted sellers.

PSA’s 2025 fraud report also identified Pokemon as its most frequently counterfeited category and said counterfeit Pokemon submissions increased by 125% year over year.

Some collectors have pushed back against claims that the copies are impossible to detect, pointing to details such as fugitive ink, print quality and missing security patterns. Others have called for future slabs to use NFC or RFID authentication.

#10658. Viral steak pop-up shut down after beef with neighbor over food lowered from apartment window

A viral Brooklyn steak pop-up has been shut down after complaints over its unusual setup, which saw boxed meals lowered from a second-floor apartment to customers on the sidewalk.

Some Guy’s House was launched by 24-year-old chef Chianli Hang and five friends as a limited food experiment and social media project. Instead of operating from a traditional storefront, the group used a homemade pulley system to lower steak dinners from their apartment window at 119 McKibbin Street.

The concept quickly gained attention online. Customers paid $25 for a sticker that came with a steak dinner, with the meal including steak, potatoes and spinach. The pop-up operated on Thursday and Friday evenings, with customers booking spots online before collecting their food from the street.

A post shared by Brooklyn Magazine (@brooklynmagazine)

The pop-up’s official website now says that Some Guy’s House is “no longer operating” and that orders booked for the current and following week will be refunded.

A follow-up video from Brooklyn Magazine said the business was shut down after roughly two weeks of service, with the team describing the closure as “inevitable.” The outlet also interviewed the group about the short-lived project and its sudden end.

According to The New York Post, Hang’s landlord told him that one person had filed multiple complaints with New York City’s 311 system. Six complaints were reportedly filed over the pop-up, and two resulted in written warnings from the Department of Health being sent to the landlord.

“We were really excited for the send-off. But then we got shut down,” Hang said.

A post shared by Some guy’s house (@someguyshouse119)

The group had planned to operate for another week, fulfill around 100 pre-orders and potentially hold a DJ-backed send-off. However, Hang said the landlord believed the apartment might be operating as a full-scale commercial kitchen.

The complaints remain under investigation, and it is unclear whether the operators themselves received any violations. The shutdown ends one of Brooklyn’s more unusual viral food concepts, which previously drew customers and influencers to an apartment window for steak dinners.

#10656. SpaceX wants to build AI data centers in space. Will it work?

Imagine if one company could become the railroad, electric utility and cloud-computing provider of the emerging space economy. That potential fueled excitement around the long-anticipated initial public offering of SpaceX. Investors are not simply betting on rockets anymore. They are betting on an entire orbital ecosystem.

Among the most ambitious and challenging ideas riding this wave of enthusiasm is something that sounds almost like science fiction: orbital data centers. SpaceX may be one of the most well-known companies seeking to build them, but it is not the only one.

The logic is seductive: Launch the data centers into orbit, where solar energy is abundant and land, water and local power grids are no longer constraints. As artificial intelligence drives an explosion in computing demand, companies are pitching orbital data centers as a way to escape the growing environmental and infrastructure pressures of Earth-based computing. Data centers often also face backlash from the public at having these centers located in their communities.

But there is a vast difference between launching satellites and operating an industrial-scale computing infrastructure in orbit. Space is unforgiving. Radiation damages electronics. The electronics generate enormous amounts of heat, and getting rid of that heat is surprisingly difficult in space. Repairs are extraordinarily expensive, and every pound launched into orbit still carries a significant cost.

We are engineering professors who study data center design and space systems engineering. Building a space-based data center will involve considerations from both sides.

First off, consider what goes into an Earth-based data center, like those that you’ve probably begun to see pop up everywhere. These facilities power cloud computing, video streaming, online banking, scientific computing and, increasingly, artificial intelligence. But a data center is much more than a room full of servers.

A data center needs several things to operate reliably. The first is electric power. Servers, networking equipment and storage devices consume large amounts of electricity, and that power demand is growing rapidly with AI.

The second is cooling. Almost all the electricity consumed by servers eventually becomes heat. If that heat is not removed quickly and reliably, equipment performance drops, failures increase and the data center can shut down. Cooling systems often include air handling units, chillers, cooling towers, pumps and, increasingly, liquid-cooling equipment. In many facilities, cooling is the largest energy consumer after the computing equipment itself.

The third is physical infrastructure, including the necessary land, buildings, structural support, backup power, water systems, communication networks and maintenance access. Data centers also need to be close enough to users and network backbones to provide fast digital services.

In short, Earth-based data centers are large electrical and thermal infrastructure systems built around computing hardware.

So what would it take to build these data centers in space, and why are companies finding this possibility such an interesting business proposition?

As on Earth, these data centers would require massive amounts of power. In space, this power would come from solar panels. The Sun always shines in space and can’t be blocked by clouds. However, depending on the orbit the solar panels are put in, the Earth may shadow them for some portion of the orbit.

And even the best solar cells available today can convert only about half the sunlight that hits them to electricity.

Another potential advantage found in space is cooling. The cold background of space (near minus 455 degrees Fahrenheit, or minus 270 degrees Celsius) creates an opportunity: waste heat from the data center could escape into space through radiators, keeping the electronics cool.

In principle, that design could eliminate some of the bulky and water-intensive cooling infrastructure used on Earth. However, those thermal radiators would require a large amount of surface area, and that would be in addition to the area required by the solar panels.

In space, there is no air to blow across hot equipment and help heat escape. The heat has to leave as infrared radiation, which is a relatively slow process. As a result, removing 10 megawatts of waste heat can require radiator surfaces comparable to the size of two football fields.

Space-based data centers could also avoid some of the local conflicts that come with building large data centers on the ground. Many communities resist new data center developments because of their land use, energy and water demand, and noise and environmental impact.

A space-based system would avoid competing for local land and water resources, and it would not generate neighborhood noise or require local zoning approval in the same way.

However, space is already getting crowded, and launching thousands of large orbital data centers would accelerate this issue. Orbital debris and micrometeorites are hazards because they can puncture the space data center, and a worst-case collision could destroy it and create even more space debris.

The frequency of space launches necessary to send all the equipment to orbit may also become a concern for some communities. SpaceX has had protests at its launch complex in Boca Chica, Texas, from local activists who argue that its rocket testing and launches damage the surrounding environment.

All that data would need to be sent between Earth and these data centers – and between the data centers themselves – using radio waves or laser communications systems. Although satellite constellations such as Starlink and Amazon Leo have demonstrated that doing this is possible, the amount of data sent to and from space would balloon.

These data centers, along with their solar panels and radiators, cannot be launched in one piece and would need to be assembled in space. This process would require new equipment for in-space servicing, assembly and manufacturing.

Another key challenge is the refresh cycle of computing hardware. Data center servers are not built to last forever. Operators on Earth usually replace or upgrade hardware every three to five years as chips improve, workloads change and equipment ages.

And equipment failures can require replacing components. The refresh and repair processes are relatively straightforward on Earth, where workers can physically remove and replace servers.

In space, refresh and repair becomes much harder. Hardware sent to orbit may be difficult or too expensive to upgrade. If the computing platform cannot be updated, or too many components fail, it may become obsolete long before the surrounding infrastructure reaches the end of its useful life.

In a field where performance improves so rapidly and demand from computing continues to increase, this hurdle could prove a major economic and operational challenge.

Then there is the harshness of space. These data centers would be in a near vacuum, with constant radiation hitting them. And depending on their orbit, they would go from hot when in the sunlight to cold in Earth’s shadow many times a day. All of these challenges, and more, are issues that will need to be addressed.

Despite these challenges, companies are moving forward with designing space-based data centers. SpaceX just announced the design for its AI1 Compute Satellite, which it hopes to use as an orbital data center spacecraft. However, this satellite is 100 to 1,000 times less capable than current Earth-based data centers.

Not every computing task makes sense to do in space. Many data center applications depend on fast response times and close connections to users on Earth. Financial transactions, interactive AI services and most cloud applications are extremely sensitive to delay.

More feasible early applications may be those that are less latency-sensitive and more tightly connected to space operations. Examples could include processing Earth observation data from satellites, military or intelligence data processing, scientific computing related to space missions, or specialized computing for satellites and other space assets.

In other words, the first viable space data centers may serve space-based customers before they compete with mainstream cloud data centers on Earth.

#10655. How Applicant Tracking Systems Read Resumes: 7 Checks Developers Should Make

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A resume that looks perfect on screen can look like a pile of scrambled text to a program. Applicant tracking systems (ATS) and hiring tools do not see your layout. They extract text from a file, guess where the sections are, and store what they find. If that step fails, the best experience in the world never reaches a human reader.

This matters whether you are sending your own resume or building a tool that processes thousands of them. This article walks through seven checks you can make with a few lines of Python, including one script you can run today.

A resume is a document with no guaranteed structure. One person writes "Work History", another writes "Experience", and a third uses a two-column layout that reads out of order. Any tool that processes resumes first has to turn this into predictable fields: contact details, sections, dates and skills.

Thinking in terms of a target schema helps. SitePoint's article on JSON schema design for document AI shows how the structure of the labels you define determines whether a document pipeline works. The same idea applies here: decide which fields you need before you write any extraction code.

Do not judge a resume by how it looks. Judge it by what comes out when you extract the text. SitePoint's walkthrough on building a JSON dataset from PDF documents describes a pipeline that extracts text from PDFs and then cleans up common extraction artifacts. That cleanup step exists because raw extraction is rarely tidy. Read the raw output first, and note what is broken.

PDF files store where characters are placed on a page, not what they mean. The pypdf documentation on extracting text from a PDF says this directly: there is no semantic layer, spacing is hard to get right because text is absolutely positioned, and pypdf is not OCR software, so it will never extract text from images.

Two practical results follow. A resume saved as a scanned image has no extractable text at all. And fancy layouts such as columns, text boxes and tables can come out in the wrong order.

Once you can extract text, a short script can catch the common failures. This one reads a PDF and reports whether it contains text, whether an email address is found, and which standard sections are missing:

Run it on a resume and look at the result. If has_text is false, the file is probably an image. If sections are missing, check whether your headings use unusual names. A passing result does not prove that every ATS will read the file the same way, but a failing result is a clear warning.

Different tools parse differently, so one script is only one opinion. A resume writing service such as ResumeCroc lists a free ATS resume checker among its tools, which is a quick way to see how another tool reads the same file. The linked page is a commercial service page, and every ATS behaves differently, so treat any checker as one data point and compare it with your own extraction results.

Most extraction problems come from layout. Single-column pages, standard headings, plain fonts and real text instead of images give parsers the best chance. Avoid putting contact details in headers or footers, since some tools skip them. If you are building a parser, test files with columns and tables on purpose so you know how your tool fails.

Create a folder of sample resumes: a clean one, a two-column one, a scanned one and one with unusual headings. Run your check against all of them whenever you change your parsing code. This turns "it seems to work" into something you can verify, and it makes regressions obvious.

Do all applicant tracking systems read PDFs the same way? No. Parsers differ in how they handle layout, headers and tables, so test more than one file format and more than one tool.

Is a Word file safer than a PDF? Not necessarily. Both can parse well or badly depending on layout. Test your own file instead of assuming.

Can a script guarantee my resume will pass an ATS? No. A script can find obvious problems, such as missing text or headings, but each hiring tool has its own rules.

Hiring tools read text, not layout. Define the fields you care about, extract the raw text first, understand what PDF extraction cannot do, automate basic checks, compare with an outside checker, keep formatting simple, and test against a small set of sample files. The script above is short, but it moves the question from "does it look right" to "what does a program actually see".

By reverse engineering the 2014 Renault Latitude’s firmware and exploiting some vulnerabilities, the researcher fixed their daylight savings time mismatch issue.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A security researcher has revealed how they were forced to update the time on their car infotainment system using reverse engineering techniques. Of course, invasive tech surgery shouldn’t be needed for this kind of basic routine daylight saving time tweaking task. However, Rasmus Moorats’ 2014 Renault Latitude wouldn’t allow him to adjust the time because the original navigation map SD card was missing.

Moorats had been warned. When he bought the used car, the previous owner noted that the SD card would be required to change the time on the in-car display. “I didn't really find that believable,” recalls the security researcher. They seem to have believed it was a skill issue of the prior owner and, because the maps it contained were chronically out of date, they decided to confidently decide they didn’t need the SD card...

The time to adjust non-connected clocks to daylight saving time inevitably came, and Moorats decided to adjust the in-car time display, which had become an hour out of sync. Two settings menus were available via the in-dash system. One allowed the adjustment of Bluetooth and Phonebook settings – clearly no use here. But the second settings menu wouldn’t produce any submenu. Instead, an error message "No maps detected!" popped up every time it was prodded.

With a certain set of skills under his belt, Moorats decided to “just RE it,” where RE = reverse engineer. He found out that the head unit ran a customized Linux-based TomTom operating system on a Samsung SoC. In brief, he extracted and analyzed the firmware, built a QEMU environment for the device, reversed the scripting engine, and uncovered a number of vulnerabilities affecting the system.

The breakthrough came in a brainwave, which seems to stem from experience with kernel exploit techniques during his day job. “Instead of trying to get the userland to execute our script, why don't I get the kernel to execute our script instead?” pondered Moorats. The approach worked, rewarding Moorats with root-level access to the infotainment system.

The 2014 Renault Latitude owner subsequently discovered that the date & time settings were in /mnt/flash/settings.dat in a custom binary format. Interestingly, the system “doesn't really have a concept of time zones at all,” observed Moorats in the conclusion of his blog post. “It gets the time from GPS and stores the local offset as a number of minutes. Mine was set to 180. I changed it to 120.”

#10652. Millions of exploding stars could soon reveal dark energy's secrets

Researchers led by the Institute of Cosmos Sciences of the University of Barcelona (ICCUB) have developed a new technique that could greatly improve how scientists study the expansion of the Universe and investigate the mysterious force known as dark energy.

Published in Nature Astronomy, the research introduces a framework called CIGaRS that can extract far more information from Type Ia supernovae, the powerful stellar explosions used to measure vast cosmic distances. Unlike many current approaches, the method relies mainly on imaging data rather than expensive spectroscopic observations. The advance is expected to help astronomers take full advantage of the enormous datasets that will soon arrive from next generation sky surveys, particularly those conducted by the Vera C. Rubin Observatory.

Type Ia supernovae occur when white dwarf stars explode. Because these explosions reach nearly the same intrinsic brightness, astronomers use them as "standard candles": by comparing their actual brightness with how bright they appear from Earth, researchers can calculate their distance.

These measurements played a crucial role in the discovery that the Universe is expanding at an accelerating rate. Scientists attribute that acceleration to dark energy, one of the most significant unsolved questions in modern physics.

However, there is an important complication. Type Ia supernovae are not perfectly identical.

How Host Galaxies Affect Supernova Measurements

Over the past 20 years, astronomers have found that a supernova's observed brightness is influenced by the galaxy where it occurs. Supernovae found in older or more massive galaxies can appear slightly different from those occurring in younger or less massive galaxies.

Researchers have typically accounted for these differences using relatively simple correction methods. While useful, these approximations can limit the accuracy of distance measurements and, in turn, the precision of cosmological studies.

A Unified Model of Supernovae and the Universe

The new framework addresses this challenge by modeling multiple factors simultaneously. Rather than treating each component independently, the researchers built a single, integrated model that includes the supernova explosions themselves, their host galaxies, the dust that alters their light, changes in supernova rates throughout cosmic history, and even the expansion of the Universe.

By connecting all of these ingredients within one statistical and physical framework, the team can capture relationships that are often overlooked when the pieces are analyzed separately.

"A powerful way of modelling the Universe is to simulate it ab initio in the computer using Bayesian inference," says Raúl Jiménez (ICREA-ICCUB), co-author of the study. "This provides a way to vary all possible parameters at the same time to predict what Universe we live in. Furthermore, by having this capacity, one can look into possible 'unknown unknown' systematics to understand their effect. The impact of these systematics in our inference is arguably the most important missing ingredient in current approaches to model the Universe."

Using Artificial Intelligence To Analyze the Cosmos

Building such a comprehensive model would normally require enormous computing power. To make the approach practical, the researchers turned to a modern technique called simulation-based inference.

The process begins with scientists generating large numbers of simulated universes based on physical models. A neural network (a type of artificial intelligence) then learns how the simulated observations relate to the physical properties that produced them. Once trained, the system can compare real astronomical observations with its simulations and determine the most likely underlying parameters.

This strategy makes it possible to analyze tens of thousands of supernovae simultaneously, a task that would be impractical using traditional techniques.

Accurate Galaxy Distances From Images Alone

One of the study's most significant findings is that the framework can determine galaxy distances (redshifts) with high accuracy using only imaging data.

Redshift measures how much a galaxy's light has been stretched as the Universe expands. It provides information about both the galaxy's distance and how far back in time we are observing it.

According to the researchers, the new method delivers redshift estimates with precision comparable to spectroscopic measurements, but without requiring spectra. This capability is especially important because upcoming surveys are expected to identify millions of supernova candidates, while only a small percentage can realistically receive spectroscopic follow-up observations.

Ready for the Rubin Observatory Data Deluge

The Vera C. Rubin Observatory, currently being built in Chile, is expected to begin a decade long survey of the sky in the near future. During that mission, it will discover an unprecedented number of supernovae. Roughly 99% of those objects will be observed only photometrically, meaning through images taken in different colors rather than detailed spectra.

The CIGaRS framework was specifically developed with this challenge in mind.

"Unlike other frameworks, which require analytic simplifications, our no-compromise end-to-end simulation-based inference approach is uniquely capable of extracting the full cosmological and astrophysical information from the Rubin Observatory's hard-earned data, while avoiding the pitfalls of selection and modelling biases," says Konstantin Karchev (ICCUB-SISSA Trieste), lead author of the study.

The benefits extend beyond measuring dark energy. The framework also provides new information about the origins of Type Ia supernovae themselves.

By reconstructing how supernova occurrence rates vary with the ages of stars in different galaxies, the model helps scientists investigate long standing questions about the systems that eventually produce these explosions.

The researchers found that combining physics based simulations with artificial intelligence can overcome several limitations of current cosmological methods. They estimate that the approach could improve cosmological constraints by as much as a factor of four compared with traditional techniques that depend only on a relatively small sample of spectroscopically observed supernovae.

As the Rubin Observatory prepares to usher in a new era of astronomical discovery, tools such as CIGaRS could help scientists extract the maximum amount of information from its observations and gain a deeper understanding of the Universe.

#10651. Pokemon Go Battle League – Best LAIC 2026 Cup team

The Pokemon Go LAIC 2026 Cup brings a new competitive challenge to the Go Battle League during the final stage of the Twilight Trails season, with trainers battling under standard Great League rules.

With a 1,500 CP limit and no type restrictions, the Latin America International Championships Cup allows some of the strongest PvP Pokemon to compete, making team composition and move coverage essential.

Here are the best Pokemon and teams for the LAIC 2026 Cup, including recommended movesets to help you climb the ranks.

One of the best teams for the LAIC 2026 Cup includes Cetitan, Swalot, and Crustle, three of the strongest Pokemon that cover most common opponents.

Another team that players could try out is Froslass, Toxapex, and Shadow Persian.

As with any League or Cup, it’s impossible to say what a true “best” team looks like in the LAIC 2026 Cup, as it really depends on the Pokemon your opponent sends out – and you won’t know that until the battle begins.

Still, there are a few Pokemon that can perform well in most situations, which we’ve listed below alongside their optimal movesets and weaknesses.

Even though Grumpig doesn’t have impressive bulk, this Pokemon is a great choice for this Cup as it offers wide coverage and decent, solid stats.

While Charge Beam is a good fast-charge Fast Move, Psywave is way better, as it also benefits from STAB. Pair it with the Charged Move Dynamic Punch. It is cheap and can expand – even more – this Pokemon’s coverage.

As a secondary Charged Move, go for Shadow Ball. It is actually not expensive at all, and it is a Ghost-type nuke that will leave your Grumpig protected against several opponents.

Ever since it got access to a good moveset during the January 2022 Community Day, Walrein has risen to the top tier of various formats in the Go Battle League, and this year’s LAIC 2026 Cup is arguably where it shines the brightest.

To use this strong beast, you’ll need Powder Snow as a Fast Move, as this gives Walrein quick enough energy to access two powerful Charged Moves: Icicle Spear, which can be spammed to take down shields, and Earthquake for huge damage and extra coverage.

Piloswine relies on a fast-paced offensive strategy, using Powder Snow to generate energy quickly and keep opponents under pressure. Its Ice/Ground typing gives it valuable protection against Electric and Poison attacks, but five weaknesses leave it vulnerable to Fighting, Fire, Grass, Steel, and Water opponents.

Icicle Spear is the go-to Charged Move, offering inexpensive Ice-type STAB to repeatedly threaten Dragon, Flying, Grass, and Ground enemies. High Horsepower packs a much heavier punch, delivering Ground-type STAB against Steel, Fire, Electric, Poison, and Rock Pokemon, making it particularly useful when Piloswine needs to land a decisive hit.

Froslass is a dangerous offensive pick that can threaten opponents from two different angles. Powder Snow generates energy quickly, allowing it to reach its powerful Charged Moves while its Ice/Ghost typing provides useful resistances to Fighting, Normal, Bug, Ice, and Poison attacks. However, five weaknesses make it vulnerable when caught in unfavorable matchups.

Avalanche delivers heavy Ice-type STAB against Dragon, Flying, Grass, and Ground Pokemon, while Shadow Ball brings equally threatening Ghost damage against Psychic and opposing Ghost-types. With both attacks capable of dealing serious damage, Froslass can force difficult shield decisions and become especially dangerous when opponents have no protection left.

Dragonair doesn’t need powerful Charged Moves to make its presence felt, as Dragon Breath delivers relentless STAB damage that can quickly wear down opponents. Its pure Dragon typing also resists Electric, Fire, Grass, and Water attacks, although Fairy, Ice, and opposing Dragon creatures remain dangerous matchups.

Wrap gives Dragonair an inexpensive Normal-type attack for maintaining pressure and forcing shields, while Aqua Tail adds Water coverage against Fire, Ground, and Rock opponents. Both moves are relatively quick to access, allowing Dragonair to keep attacking while Dragon Breath does most of the heavy lifting.

Toxapex can make opponents work hard for every bit of damage, combining exceptional bulk with eight resistances that help it survive prolonged battles. Bite adds steady Dark-type damage against Ghost and Psychic opponents, including Psychic-types that threaten it, although its limited energy generation makes Charged Moves harder to reach.

Brine offers Water-type STAB to chip away at Fire, Ground, and Rock opponents, while Sludge Wave delivers a much heavier Poison-type hit against Fairy and Grass creatures. Both attacks require patience, so Toxapex is best suited to matchups where its durability can compensate for its slower offensive pace.

Shelgon is a surprisingly bulky Dragon-type that relies on its solid defenses and consistent damage rather than overwhelming offensive stats. Its useful resistances let it comfortably take on common Fire, Water, Grass, and Electric-types while slowly wearing opponents down.

Dragon Breath is the ideal Fast Move thanks to its high STAB damage and constant pressure. Twister is the cheaper Charged Move, allowing Shelgon to bait shields and chip away at opponents, while Flamethrower provides valuable coverage against Steel-types that would otherwise resist its Dragon-type attacks.

Lunatone has an unusual Rock/Psychic typing that offers useful protection against Fire, Flying, Normal, Poison, and Psychic attacks, but its seven weaknesses make choosing the right matchup essential. Psywave supplies Psychic-type STAB damage while generating energy, allowing Lunatone to keep its Charged Moves within reach.

Weather Ball (Ice) gives Lunatone a quick answer to Dragon, Flying, Grass, and Ground Pokemon, including two types that exploit its weaknesses. Rock Slide adds stronger STAB damage against Fire, Flying, Bug, and Ice opponents, making it a valuable option for pressuring shields or securing knockouts.

This Pokemon works best as a lead or team charger. Plus, it has the necessary Defense to stand its ground while dealing good damage.

Astonish is a very spammy move that will allow it to access its Charged Moves fast while also getting rid of the opponent’s shields. The key to Dusknoir making it into the League is mainly because of Shadow Punch, an excellent Ghost-type move, and Dynamic Punch, a Fighting-type attack that expands its coverage.

Abomasnow is at its best when it can keep opponents on the defensive, using Powder Snow to generate energy quickly and fire off repeated Charged Moves. Its Grass/Ice typing gives it useful resistances to Water, Electric, Grass, and Ground, but seven weaknesses, including a double vulnerability to Fire, make unfavorable matchups especially punishing.

Weather Ball (Ice) is the main source of pressure, delivering quick STAB damage against Dragon, Flying, Grass, and Ground enemies. Energy Ball provides heavier Grass-type coverage for Water, Rock, and Ground opponents, with a chance to lower their Defense and make subsequent attacks even more threatening.

Besides its great bulk, Lapras has an impressive move pool, with four Fast Moves and seven Charged Moves to pick from.

Even though focusing only on Water and Ice moves to benefit from STAB would be the logical thing to do, for the Fast Move, it is best to go with Psywave. It offers the most energy generation out of all the options, and it expands Lapras’s coverage.

Skull Bash, Blizzard, and Hydro Pump are quite expensive moves, and with a few other options available, they are just not worth it. Instead, use Sparkling Aria for a solid Charged Move with STAB. It costs the same as Surf but does five more damage.

As for the secondary Charged Move, Ice Beam will offer more coverage against Grass, Dragon, and Flying opponents while also benefiting from STAB.

Aurorus made it to the list mainly because of its outstanding Stamina (214) and Ice typing, which is offensively valuable as it hits a specific niche.

This dual Rock/Ice-type Pokemon works ideally as a lead, as it can push the enemy shields with its spammy Fast Move Powder Snow and then devastate them with Weather Ball or the nuke Meteor Beam, depending on the coverage.

Crustle has never been a PvP star in Pokemon Go, but the new meta and the addition of Rock Wrecker to its move pool allowed it to rise in the Battle League.

Fury Cutter is the optimal Fast Move for energy generation. Then, with a combination of X-Scissor (used to bait enemy shields) and Rock Wrecker (strong and very cheap) as Charged Moves, Crustle will be able to take down plenty of the cup’s biggest players like Aurorus and Swalot with no problem at all.

Swalot can be a nuisance for opponents that rely on Fairy, Fighting, or Grass attacks, using its pure Poison typing and solid bulk to withstand damage. Infestation prioritizes energy generation over raw power, giving Swalot time to build toward its Charged Moves while keeping its Ground and Psychic weaknesses in mind.

Sludge provides Poison-type STAB to punish Fairy and Grass Pokemon, while Ice Beam offers a much more unexpected threat. Its Ice coverage can catch Dragon, Flying, Grass, and Ground opponents for super-effective damage, including Ground-types that would otherwise have a favorable matchup against Swalot.

Cetitan makes up for its limited defensive typing with impressive HP and a fast-paced moveset. Powder Snow generates energy quickly, letting it threaten opponents with repeated Ice-type attacks, although its weaknesses to Fighting, Fire, Rock, and Steel leave it with several dangerous matchups.

Icicle Spear is the go-to Charged Move, offering cheap Ice-type STAB that can wear down Dragon, Flying, Grass, and Ground opponents. Superpower adds much-needed Fighting coverage against Steel, Rock, and Ice-types, but its Attack and Defense debuffs make timing crucial, especially when Cetitan needs to stay in battle.

The LAIC 2026 Cup has a 1,500 CP limit, with Fire, Dark, Steel, and Fairy-type Pokemon banned. Legendaries, Mythicals, and Ultra Beasts are also ineligible.

Unlike the in-person Latin America International Championships, the Go Battle League version does not allow Mega Evolutions.

#10648. Quantum mechanics once baffled scientists. Now it's changing the world

For much of the early 20th century, quantum mechanics was one of the most puzzling ideas in science. The theory challenged conventional thinking and left even leading physicists struggling to make sense of its implications. A century later, it has become the foundation of technologies that influence daily life, including lasers, microchips, secure communications, and emerging quantum computers.

In a new perspective article published in Science, Dr. Marlan Scully of Texas A&M University reflects on the remarkable evolution of quantum mechanics, from an abstract theory about tiny particles to a powerful framework helping researchers tackle some of the most difficult questions in science.

"Quantum mechanics started as a way to explain the behavior of tiny particles," said Scully, who is also affiliated with Princeton University. "Now it's driving innovations that were unimaginable just a generation ago."

Scully has played a major role in advancing the field. He co-authored the influential textbook Quantum Optics, a resource that has educated generations of physicists. His research in coherent nanoscale laser spectroscopy helped make it possible to study molecules with atomic-scale precision. He has also developed groundbreaking concepts involving quantum heat engines, which challenge traditional assumptions about thermodynamic efficiency and may one day lead to new energy technologies.

From Schrödinger's Cat to Quantum Technology

One of the most famous illustrations of quantum mechanics came in 1935, when Erwin Schrödinger proposed his cat paradox. The thought experiment suggested that a cat could exist in a state that is both alive and dead until it is observed. Schrödinger introduced the idea to highlight how strange quantum theory appeared.

Today, those once-bizarre concepts have moved far beyond philosophical debates.

"That 'quantum weirdness' is no longer just a philosophical puzzle," said Scully. "It's the foundation of quantum computing, quantum cryptography and even gravitational wave detection."

The foundations of quantum mechanics were built by pioneers including Schrödinger and Werner Heisenberg. They developed two different mathematical approaches, wave mechanics and matrix mechanics, to describe quantum systems. Over time, these approaches were unified and contributed to the development of quantum field theory, which explains how particles interact through electromagnetic and nuclear forces.

Their work expanded on Niels Bohr's early atomic model, which pictured electrons orbiting the nucleus much like planets orbit the sun. While later discoveries refined that picture, Bohr's model helped pave the way for modern quantum theory.

Among the most important concepts in quantum mechanics is quantum coherence. This phenomenon allows particles such as atoms and photons to remain linked in a coordinated state, even across significant distances.

Quantum coherence led directly to the development of the laser, a technology that many once believed could never work. Today, lasers are used throughout modern society, from supermarket barcode scanners to vision correction procedures and advanced scientific instruments.

Coherence is also closely tied to quantum entanglement, the phenomenon that prompted Albert Einstein to describe it as "spooky action at a distance."

Entanglement enables particles to share information through uniquely quantum properties. These effects form the basis of quantum encryption systems and improve the sensitivity of sophisticated instruments such as the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (LIGO), which detects tiny ripples in spacetime.

Quantum Heat Engines Challenge Classical Limits

One of the more surprising applications of quantum physics involves quantum heat engines.

Traditional engines are constrained by the Carnot Limit, which defines the maximum efficiency allowed by classical thermodynamics. Researchers have found that by exploiting quantum coherence, it may be possible to create engines that exceed those classical limits.

"It's a striking example of how quantum principles can rewrite the rules of classical physics," Scully said.

The influence of quantum mechanics now extends far beyond physics.

In biology, techniques such as coherent Raman spectroscopy allow researchers to examine viruses and other structures at the nanoscale, providing valuable insights into the microscopic world.

Quantum ideas are also shaping efforts to understand the universe itself. Scientists working on concepts such as string theory and quantum gravity are attempting to reconcile quantum mechanics with Einstein's theory of relativity, one of the biggest unsolved problems in modern physics.

Researchers are even applying quantum concepts to the long-standing challenge of understanding turbulence. The chaotic motion of air and fluids affects weather patterns, climate systems, and aircraft performance. By studying superfluid helium, a substance that displays unusual quantum behavior, scientists are uncovering patterns that could improve climate modeling, storm prediction, and aviation safety.

Despite a century of success, quantum mechanics continues to raise profound questions.

Can gravity be quantized (i.e., does gravity behave like other forces at the quantum level)? Could quantum computers transform medicine and materials science? What new insights about the universe might emerge from future quantum technologies?

Scully believes the search for answers is only beginning.

"At the start of the 20th century, many thought physics was complete," he said. "Now, in the 21st century, we know the adventure is just beginning."

Five Ways Quantum Mechanics Affects Everyday Life

#10647. Hidden Valley Ranch will pay for your wedding if you can prove your love for ranch

Hidden Valley Ranch is giving one lucky couple the chance to get married for free, with an all-expenses-paid wedding that brings together football, Valentine’s Day, and plenty of ranch dressing.

The company announced its “A Match Made in Hidden Valley” contest on November 10, offering engaged couples across the US the opportunity to win a wedding in Los Angeles for themselves and 50 guests.

The giveaway comes as Valentine’s Day and the Super Bowl fall on the same day in 2027, prompting Hidden Valley Ranch to combine the two occasions into one celebration.

Couples interested in winning the wedding can enter the contest between November 19 and December 4, 2026, through the official Hidden Valley Wedding website.

To qualify, eligible engaged couples must complete an entry form, answer five short essay questions, and submit a video lasting no longer than 90 seconds through Google Drive or an unlisted YouTube link.

Applicants are encouraged to share their relationship stories and explain why they want to celebrate Valentine’s Day and the Super Bowl together. Hidden Valley Ranch is also looking for couples who can demonstrate how the brand has played a role in their relationship or game-day traditions.

The winning couple will be notified on or around December 14, giving them approximately two months to prepare for their February 14, 2027 wedding.

The prize includes a wedding celebration in Los Angeles for 50 guests, with travel, accommodations, and wedding attire provided for the couple. Hidden Valley Ranch will also cover the venue, catering, drinks, and event arrangements.

The ceremony will take place before kickoff, followed by a traditional wedding reception and a selection of game-day foods paired with Hidden Valley Ranch.

#10644. Pokemon VGC competitor claims he was wrongfully suspended after another player used his identity at Worlds

A Pokemon VGC competitor claims he was wrongfully suspended after another player used his tournament identity at the 2026 Pokemon World Championships.

Johnny Chiou made the claim in a lengthy post on X, saying his friend Chen-Wei Liu discovered that his RK9 account had been transferred to another email address without his permission.

According to Chiou, another player later appeared at Worlds using Player ID 5283777, a number Liu says was assigned to him and used during the 2024 Pokemon World Championships. Liu reported the issue to Pokemon support, but was later issued an indefinite suspension for deception related to his Worlds qualification and attendance.

We Demand Transparency and Justice for CHEN-WEI LIU. @playpokemon My friend, CHEN-WEI LIU, discovered that his RK9 account had been transferred to another email address without his knowledge or authorization. This raised serious concerns that his qualification for the 2026…

A Player ID is a unique number used to track a competitor’s tournament history, results and qualifications. Pokemon’s official rules say players must have their own personal Player ID and use only one number.

The supporting timeline says Liu noticed on September 4 that his RK9 profile and tournament history had disappeared. He contacted RK9 the following day and later provided the Player ID he had used at the 2024 Worlds.

The evidence package includes a photograph of a match slip from August 28, the first day of the 2026 Worlds VGC competition. It lists I-Shang Chang from Taiwan against Jin Yang Lee, with Player ID 5283777 printed under Chang’s name. Public VGC standings also list the match.

Chiou’s post refers to the player as I-Hsiang Chang, while the match slip and public standings spell the name I-Shang Chang.

The timeline says RK9 confirmed on September 17 that Liu’s account had been moved to a new email address before Worlds after an email-change request was submitted with the correct credentials. Liu allegedly replied that he never requested or authorized the transfer.

Liu then contacted The Pokemon Company International on September 20 and asked for an investigation. He followed up in October, according to the timeline, but says he received no meaningful explanation.

2024 Pokemon world champion among three “banned” from Worlds over Pokemon Center line dispute

Pokemon VGC competitor demands better hygiene after smelly player made him throw up

Pokemon pro sparks controversy after “cheating” at official VGC tournament

On October 16, Pokemon issued Liu a disciplinary notice under case DISINC-007883. The notice said the alleged violation concerned his “qualification and attendance for the 2026 Pokemon World Championships.”

It cited Section 4.3 of the Pokemon Standards of Conduct and listed:

“Deception, defrauding, or engagement of a fellow program participant under false pretenses.”

The notice suspended Liu indefinitely from Play Pokemon events, including both competing and attending as a spectator. It also said he could submit an appeal after 90 days, beginning January 13, 2027.

However, the notice does not explain what Pokemon believes Liu actually did. It does not say whether the company believes he knowingly allowed another person to use his account, misrepresented his identity, participated in a qualification scheme or misled tournament staff.

The timeline says Liu submitted a formal rebuttal on October 17 and followed up five days later. According to the material posted by Chiou, no response had arrived by November 10.

The dispute follows several other Play Pokemon controversies covered by Dexerto this year, including a former Pokemon World Champion who said he was barred from Worlds after a Pokemon Center line dispute, a Pokemon TCG veteran who said he was banned for life after calling out a judge, and a Pokemon Go champion who challenged the decision to strip his Orlando Regional title.

For now, the public record leaves two competing explanations. Liu says someone else may have used his account and tournament identity. Pokemon’s notice indicates that it believes Liu was involved in deception, but does not publicly explain how.

#10643. How to Quickly Check What Your HTML Code Looks Like in a Browser

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Writing HTML is one of the main parts of building a website. It is mainly responsible for webpage structure and content.

A small error can result in layout problems. Oftentimes, you don't notice these issues until you preview the page in a browser. A quick way to ensure that your layout looks the same as you want is to preview your HTML code.

In this blog, we’ll show you easy ways to check how your HTML code will look in real time. So keep on reading till the end.

The following are two easy ways to check how your HTML code will look in real time.

This is a simple way to preview your HTML. You don't need a web server to preview your HTML code. You have to follow the following steps.

Open a code editor or simply Notepad on your device. Create a new file and paste your HTML inside it.

Step 2 - Save the File With an HTML Extension

After adding your HTML code in Notepad, save the file as index.html. You have to ensure that the extension is .html, not .txt.

If you are using Notepad on Windows, click on “File” and navigate to the “Save As” option and click it. Then enter index.html as the filename. Make sure that Notepad doesn’t save it as a text document.

Locate the saved file on your device. Double-click to open it in your default browser. The browser will render the HTML elements to show the headings, paragraphs, and buttons on the page, as you can see in the image below.

This is how you can create a simple file to preview your HTML before deploying it. If you see any errors, you can correct them in your file and preview it again.

However, it is worth considering that HTML may not show the complete website behavior alone. The final result can also depend on JavaScript, external CSS, or other resources. You should check those files as well.

This method provides an easy way to preview your HTML code. It involves using a specialized online HTML viewer. This approach is even quicker and doesn't even require you to create a local file first.

Step 1 - Open the HTML Viewer Open your web browser and search for an HTML viewer. You may see multiple tools in the search results. Select one that allows HTML preview online. For demonstration purposes, we are using HTML Viewer by minifier.org.

Once you’ve selected the tool, open it. Navigate to its input box and paste your HTML code into it. We are using the same HTML code from the first example.

You can also upload your file or paste its URL into the tool. After entering your HTML code, click on the “View” button to preview your HTML code.

In the screenshot above, you can see the tool showing the HTML preview on the right side. This tool also gives you the option to edit your HTML code and see the results in real time through the “Auto-update” option.

If the auto-update option is checked, you can see the changes in real time as you edit the code. This makes editing much easier, as you can modify the code and preview the changes immediately without returning to your original file. It also allows you to verify how your layout will appear on desktop, tablet, or mobile. You can check this by clicking on the icons provided in the top right corner of the tool. Once you are satisfied with the output, you can copy or download your edited HTML file easily.

This tool also allows you to test the HTML code of your game or video in real time, as you can see in the screenshot below.

These features make such specialized HTML viewers practical. These are quick and easy to use. However, the features shown above may not be available on all the tools. If you are specifically looking for such features, you can read the tool’s description for these features before using it.

HTML is one of the main components of a website. It defines the structure and content of webpages. Many users need to check how their HTML code will look in a browser to identify potential issues before deployment.

To preview your HTML code, you can use simple methods. One is to paste your code into Notepad and save it as index.html. Then open it in your browser to get a preview of your HTML code.

You can also use a specialized HTML viewer. Such tools can work by just pasting the code into the input box. Once you paste your code, click on the view button to get a preview of your HTML code. Some tools also offer various other features, such as editing, viewing games, and videos in real time.

Both of these methods work fine. The choice depends on the user's preferences and needs.

The open-source project reportedly violates Synaptics' patents, but its creator begs to differ.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A hobbyist building on open-source driver for DisplayLink hardware received a cease-and-desist from Synaptics, resulting in a lengthy written argument and a threat to sue from the company. According to Phoronix, the Vino driver was “clean-room reverse-engineered” and partly developed using AI and written in Rust. However, even though the person behind the open-source driver, Mike Lothian, did not break the copyright of the code behind the driver, Synaptics argued that his work violates its patent on the DisplayLink technology.

The story began in July 2026, when Lothian reached out to Łukasz Spintzyk, a software engineer working at Synaptics, to help solve a few bugs he’s been encountering. However, Michal Lukaszek, the Strategic Engineering Partnerships Lead at the company, replied a couple of weeks later, saying that the company is concerned that Lothian is attempting to implement the DisplayLink protocol itself, which is a violation of its patents. This resulted in a cease-and-desist letter from Synaptics’ legal department asking him to take down the Vino GitHub repo, among other things.

Synaptics claims that Lothian’s work infringes on two patents: GB2484736 and GB2485613. The former, called Image generation, is about sending screen updates over a general-purpose data network like USB or Ethernet using a specific architecture and compression method, while the latter, called Display control device, details hardware that works with compressed data and only decompresses it as needed. Lothian responded, asking for complete details as to how his work infringes on its patents, but received no response, prompting him to follow up three weeks later.

This was when Synaptics decided to escalate, telling him that it would be billing Lothian “to recoup the cost and effort required to create such documentation of your infringing acts.” Andrew Bateman, the company’s Assistant General Counsel, also added, “By open sourcing our DisplayLink technology for whatever personal reasons you may have as a ‘hobbyist,’ you will be single-handedly eviscerating DisplayLink's competitive advantage in this crowded market by educating our competitors and other third parties as to how we implement our proprietary technology, which we have gone to great lengths and great expense to prevent.”

“If you'd like to notify the media or otherwise publicize our response, I encourage you to do so. We welcome any and all free publicity to let the world (in particular, our competitors and our shareholders) know that Synaptics aggressively defends and protects its DisplayLink IP from all threats of infringement.”

Lothian eventually took the GitHub repo containing the Vino driver offline, but it seems that the fight isn’t over yet. The hobbyist claims that Synaptics’ patents are invalid, saying, “In both cases the independent claims as filed contained no network or transport limitation. The claims were granted only after being amended to add delivery of the display data over a ‘general-purpose data network’ (and, for GB2485613, a ‘transport protocol’ with an ‘unpackaging’ step). That added feature was not new.”

He further argues that even though the company says that DisplayLink isn’t part of the Open Invention Network, Synaptics itself is an OIN licensee. Some say that an OIN license requires that any subsidiary acquired by the original licensee and all its patents would also fall under the company’s OIN license, although Synaptics apparently disagrees with this.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Despite the escalation, Lothian says that he remains open to discussing a sensible resolution. But unless the two parties come to an agreement, it looks like they’re getting ready for a legal face-off. You can see the complete email thread between Lothian and Synaptics in this Linux Kernel Mailing List page and the attached email thread (PDF).

Lothian said that he used a Claude subscription to help out with his cleanroom reverse-engineering efforts, revealing the headache that advanced AI tools pose for tech giants. A user has created a free Adobe Creative Suite clone in Rust using Claude, and was also reportedly working on an open-source office suite and Autodesk tools. Aside from that, we’ve also seen a lot of reverse-engineered games running on platforms they’re not designed for, forcing Anthropic to enforce some limitations on Opus 5.5. There was also concern that the widespread use of AI in chipmaking could result in the inadvertent spread of a copied design or an infringed patent across thousands of chips before anyone catches it.

#10640. Scientists discovered the brain doesn't make decisions the way we thought

Scientists at the University of Illinois Urbana Champaign have uncovered evidence that could reshape how researchers think about both the brain and artificial intelligence. Their findings suggest that decision making begins much earlier in the brain than traditional theories propose, offering fresh ideas for designing future AI systems that are more capable and far more energy efficient.

Led by electrical and computer engineering professor Yurii Vlasov at The Grainger College of Engineering, the research was published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Science (PNAS). The study points to an unexpected role for early sensory brain regions in decision making, challenging the long accepted view that decisions emerge only after information moves through a strict hierarchy of brain regions.

The human brain is widely regarded as the most complex structure in the known universe. Scientists still do not fully understand how it works, which is why reverse engineering the brain was identified by the National Academy of Engineering in 2008 as one of the 14 grand challenges for engineering in the 21st century.

For decades, many artificial intelligence systems, including convolutional neural networks, have been inspired by the idea that the brain processes information in a one way sequence. According to this traditional model, sensory information travels upward through increasingly complex brain regions until it reaches the frontal cortex, where decisions are made.

Vlasov and other researchers have increasingly questioned whether that picture is complete.

Instead, they are exploring a model based on natural intelligence, which has been refined through evolution over hundreds of millions of years. In this framework, the brain does not rely only on a step by step flow of information. Decision making also depends on interconnected feedback loops that allow information to move in both directions between brain regions.

Because biological intelligence performs remarkably complex tasks while using far less energy than today's AI systems, understanding this architecture could help guide the development of future artificial intelligence.

"We want to learn from a billion years of evolution," Vlasov said. "How is that biological intelligence organized architecturally? Can we learn from the architectural side of the brain and emulate that to make AI more effective, less power hungry, and more intelligent than it currently is? In the level of decision-making, that's where current AI is lacking."

Early Brain Regions Show Decision Making Activity

To investigate how these processes work, the research team focused on the brain's earliest stages of sensing and perception.

The scientists recorded neural activity in mice as they navigated a virtual reality corridor and made perceptual decisions. They found evidence of decision related activity in the primary somatosensory cortex (S1), one of the brain's earliest sensory processing areas.

Rather than simply passing information forward, S1 appeared to be influenced by higher brain regions through feedback loops. This top down regulation suggests that decision making involves continuous communication across multiple brain areas instead of a simple one direction flow of information.

"The neural code of the brain is still mostly an unknown language," Vlasov said. "But this systems-level understanding can be viewed as a potential impact on how more efficient artificial neural networks can be built -- how the next generation of AI can be thought through. Maybe with these analogies that we learn from real brains, we can improve AI further."

What the Findings Could Mean for Future AI

The researchers emphasize that the study does not provide a blueprint for building better artificial intelligence. Instead, it offers new insights into how the brain organizes decision making that could eventually inspire future AI architectures.

Next, Vlasov and his team plan to investigate the timing of these brain signals in greater detail. They also intend to develop new technologies for measuring neural activity to better understand how feedback loops emerge and coordinate different levels of brain processing.

"By looking at the fast temporal dynamics of neural activity, maybe we can understand better how these feedback loops are engaged in making decisions," Vlasov said. "Maybe that's the approach that potentially uncovers these currently unknown mechanisms -- how these feedback loops are organized dynamically and how they form and shape different levels of processing. Maybe that can be implemented in new architectures for AI."

#10636. Influencer uses his 1.1M followers to track down stolen $500K McLaren

A Detroit influencer managed to recover his stolen $500,000 McLaren after using his 1.1 million social media followers to track it down, but not before thieves were caught doing donuts in the luxury supercar.

Businessman and content creator Ali Sobh was left stunned when his rare McLaren disappeared from the driveway behind his home in Detroit’s Boston-Edison neighborhood.

However, things took an even stranger turn when footage surfaced online showing someone driving his stolen vehicle at a street takeover, performing donuts in front of a crowd of spectators.

Rather than simply waiting for police to locate the car, Sobh decided to put his massive social media following to work.

According to ClickOnDetroit, Sobh shared footage of the stolen vehicle with his 1.1 million followers and asked for help identifying its whereabouts.

The footage, also highlighted by FOX 2 Detroit, showed the McLaren being driven recklessly at a street takeover, with the driver spinning the expensive vehicle around in front of onlookers.

A post shared by Ali Sobh (@alisobh_official)

Fortunately, Sobh’s followers came through with tips that helped narrow down the car’s location.

The influencer passed a potential location near Six Mile and Telegraph to Detroit police, who subsequently recovered the $500,000 supercar.

Sobh explained that the vehicle was particularly special because of its rare paint job.

“I’m the only one in the country that has this color as well,” he told ClickOnDetroit.

Although he managed to recover the vehicle, Sobh was understandably frustrated that the thieves had been brazen enough to show it off at a public gathering.

#10635. Alan Turing's biggest AI assumption may have been wrong

Alan Turing's famous ideas about artificial intelligence may have sent AI research down the wrong path for the past 75 years, according to prominent computer scientist Peter J. Denning.

In his new book, Turing's Mistake: Escaping the Yoke of Unintelligent Machines, Denning argues that two foundational assumptions made by Turing in 1950 continue to shape AI research today. The first is that intelligence can exist independently of a physical body and therefore be recreated in computer software. The second is that a machine can demonstrate intelligence by successfully imitating a human in conversation, an idea that later became known as the Turing test.

"These two claims have shaped much of AI research and development," Denning writes. "My premise is that our acquiescence to these claims has led to the AI mess in which we find ourselves today."

Denning argues that pursuing artificial general intelligence (AGI), or machines with human level intelligence, is unlikely to succeed. Instead, he warns, the technologies society is building could introduce significant new risks.

At the heart of Denning's argument is the idea of tacit knowledge, the vast amount of human understanding that cannot easily be put into words or represented in a form that computers can process.

He says machine learning cannot capture five major categories of tacit knowledge: common sense, everyday interactions with people and the environment, emotions and perception, practical performance skills, and the social and historical knowledge embedded in culture.

Researchers have long attempted to organize common sense into databases. One of the best known efforts was Douglas Lenat's Cyc project, which began in the 1980s with the goal of creating an extensive collection of common sense facts. After four decades of work, the project contained roughly 25 million entries.

"Yet even this treasury could not add up to a background of common sense sufficient to make expert systems smart enough to be experts," Denning notes. "Cyc validated that much of the knowledge that makes people experts cannot be articulated as propositions."

Denning believes practical skills present an even greater challenge.

"Our performance skills in thousands of domains cannot be communicated to machines," he explains. "Whereas descriptions of skillful outcomes ('know what') can often be represented as bits and stored in a machine, we do not know how to encode the embodied knowledge for skillful performance ('know how')."

He points to accomplished musicians as an example.

"A virtuoso violinist can play beautiful music yet cannot describe to an acolyte how to produce it.

"Even if a robot could observe and imitate skilled humans, having no biological body, a robot cannot grasp how the musician feels when playing beautiful music or how an audience feels when hearing it."

Denning also includes intuition, gut feelings, imagination, and spontaneous creativity among the forms of tacit knowledge that remain beyond the reach of machines.

Denning argues that all of these limitations stem from what he calls the "representation problem."

Computers can only perform calculations using data and instructions that have been encoded into physical forms they can recognize and process. Tacit knowledge, however, does not naturally fit into that framework.

"Behind every word is a deep well of tacit knowledge that gives it meaning," Denning says. "Words are but symbolic representations of meanings, not the meanings themselves. Commonly used Large Language Models, such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini only manipulate words, they cannot know or understand the meaning of what they are saying."

According to Denning, this creates a fundamental divide. Because scientists still cannot fully explain how tacit knowledge works in humans, they also cannot translate it into a form machines can use.

"How we host tacit knowledge is largely a mystery," Denning admits. "All we know is that it is embodied. We have no idea what we might observe and measure in our bodies to reveal it."

Denning also argues that intelligence depends heavily on context, the surrounding circumstances that give words, actions, and decisions their meaning.

Context allows people to recognize sarcasm, humor, sincerity, and emotion. It helps determine when to be diplomatic, when to joke, and how to interpret countless social cues.

"When you inquire into where an assumption of the current context came from, you discover it rests on previous conversations from previous contexts. Each of those in turn rests on further previous conversations and their contexts. This pattern is endless and fractal," Denning explains.

Culture presents another major obstacle for AI.

Denning describes culture as encompassing values, norms, judgments, history, communities, moods, and even relationships involving power and care.

"Human conversations are imbued with background assumptions that give meaning and relevance to the words being used," Denning explains.

"Scaling up LLMs with ever larger neural networks will not enable them to acquire the embodied human knowledge we call culture. LLMs will not attain the objective of the Turing test: to demonstrate machine thought indistinguishable from human thought."

AI Safety and the Limits of Human Understanding

Denning concludes that humans and AI systems may ultimately develop different forms of tacit knowledge that neither can fully understand.

"Machines cannot read our tacit knowledge and we cannot read theirs," he writes. "We are aliens across an uncrossable divide."

He argues this gap raises serious concerns about AI safety. If machines cannot interpret the unspoken context behind human intentions, reliably aligning advanced AI systems with human goals may prove impossible.

"Through AI automation, agentic networks of machines are likely to develop their own machine intelligence that does not reach the level of human general intelligence but is still quite capable of creating severe problems for humans. This threat is a greater than a take-over by superintelligent machines," he explains.

"Machine intelligence has different concerns from us and does not appear to care about us. Its ways of thinking and problem-solving look alien to us. We do not yet know how to live safely with these machines.

"Pulling back from an AI automation singularity will demand much from us. We start by accepting that the familiar culture is fading away as intelligent machines appear in our society and we do not know what is coming. We decline to think like machines or be subservient to machines. We refuse to submit to a yoke imposed by low-intelligence machines. Most importantly, we reassert our humanity, declare once again what makes us different from machines, and celebrate those differences."

Materials provided by Taylor & Francis Group. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#10633. Florida woman arrested after targeting ex’s Pokemon cards because he wasn’t giving her attention

A Florida woman has been arrested after allegedly targeting her ex-boyfriend’s Pokemon card collection during an argument, before returning to his apartment for a bong and ending up facing felony charges.

Nadia Hussain, 23, was arrested in Orlando on November 7 following a bizarre confrontation involving Pokemon cards, a cellphone, and an interrupted 911 call.

According to an Orlando Police Department arrest affidavit obtained by Guessing Headlights, Hussain had spent the night at her ex-boyfriend’s apartment before the pair got into an argument.

Her ex, Jordan Bonilla, asked her to leave, but she allegedly refused, prompting him to begin recording the confrontation.

Police say Hussain knocked the phone from his hand, struck him several times, and repeatedly demanded that he “delete the video!”

She then turned her attention to his Pokemon card collection, which was sitting on the living room table.

According to WFTV, Hussain later admitted to police that she deliberately grabbed the cards after realizing how much it upset her ex-boyfriend.

She also told investigators she had been purposefully annoying him because she felt he wasn’t showing her enough affection.

Bonilla eventually escorted Hussain to her car before rushing back upstairs and locking his apartment door.

However, the encounter wasn’t over. Hussain returned, claiming she had left her bong inside.

Despite promising not to enter, she allegedly forced her way into the apartment when Bonilla opened the door to hand it over.

Police say she headed straight toward the living room before Bonilla blocked her path. She then entered a bathroom with a second entrance to the living room, leading him to believe she was attempting to reach his Pokemon cards again.

Chainsaw-wielding Florida man arrested for breaking into store and stealing $12K in Pokemon cards

Pokemon collector secretly put GPS tracker on woman’s car to find trading card restocks

Pokemon card collector sets up alleged thieves after they relist his stolen cards online

When Bonilla tried calling 911, Hussain allegedly struck his phone several times to prevent the call. Police confirmed dispatchers received a 911 hang-up from his number.

Neighbors eventually intervened and helped remove her from the apartment.

Hussain was arrested and charged with domestic battery and witness tampering to hinder communication with law enforcement, the latter being a third-degree felony.

Despite all the chaos surrounding the Pokemon collection, no theft charges involving the cards were filed.

It’s hardly the first bizarre incident involving Pokemon cards this year. In May, a Florida man was arrested after allegedly using a chainsaw to steal $12,000 worth of cards.

More recently, the FBI began investigating thieves using stolen credit cards to purchase rare Pokemon cards from trading card stores.

In Hussain’s case, there is no indication that any Pokemon cards were stolen or damaged, although the confrontation has left her facing criminal charges. The allegations have not been proven in court.
